item.title: Quantifying Linepack Storage Potential of Hydrogen Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.40822v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Future hydrogen systems depend on large-scale storage to balance supply and demand. Hydrogen networks can store energy in the pipelines themselves, but the potential of this linepack storage has not been quantified comparably to dedicated storage facilities. We transfer metrics established for conventional storage, such as volume capacity and full-cycle equivalents, to hydrogen networks. To evaluate them, we formulate an optimization problem maximizing linepack storage utilization, subject to non-convex PDE-based constraints describing transient gas flow. We solve the optimization problem over a full-year horizon to capture seasonal variations and to assess the interaction with cavern storage. For computational tractability, we propose a simulation-informed sequential convex programming approach with adaptive time stepping that reduces problem size by up to 98% at accuracy comparable to fixed-resolution methods. For the GasLib-40 topology with German scenario data, the network provides a volume capacity of 24 million normal cubic meters at 28 full-cycle equivalents per year.

item.title: Dynamic Persuasion: Managing Reputation under Censored Feedback
item.description: arXiv:2610.40881v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a long-run sender who repeatedly communicates about a state to a sequence of myopic receivers and whose credibility is a public score updated from past interactions. Receivers face a lemon loss and an opportunity loss, and their behavior depends on these only through a single index, the tolerance. Because the score records only detected misrepresentations, it rests above the sender's true honesty rate; we characterize this credibility premium in closed form. In a fluid limit in which the score adjusts slowly, no policy earns more than operating at a single credibility level, and the sender's gain from managing credibility equals the value of the premium: against receivers who correct for imperfect detection, that gain vanishes. At a fixed adjustment speed, every policy is bounded by the fluid value plus a term linear in the speed. We then study three policy classes, linear, (s,S), and threshold, obtain the optimal parameters of the linear and threshold classes in closed form, show how receiver losses shape them, and show that, under an approximation, the optimal (s,S) band collapses to a threshold. Simulations of the dynamics agree with the closed forms and indicate where the single-level conclusion stops: bands pay when switching modes is costly, and cycles pay when demand is seasonal.
item.dc:creator: Ahmet E. Arcaklioglu, Ceyhun Eksin

item.title: Approximate Dynamic Programming for Link Reconfiguration to Reduce Malicious Input Controllability in Consensus Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.40919v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Communication links influence how strongly a malicious input at one sensor affects a consensus network. We study how a defender can reduce this influence by selecting one additional link after observing the currently attacked sensor. The attacked sensor changes over time, and vulnerability is measured by the trace of a finite-horizon controllability Gramian. A prescribed local epsilon-greedy attacker response rule defines a discounted Markov decision process for the defender. Exact dynamic programming (DP) provides an optimal policy using the full Gramian payoff matrix and attacker transition model. We then introduce approximate dynamic programming (ADP) that learns from sampled attacker transitions and empirical Gramian costs estimated from measured impulse responses. Under conditionally unbiased costs and standard sampling and learning-rate conditions, the learned action-value table converges to the exact DP solution. The analysis uses Bellman contraction and bounds the effect of persistent Gramian estimation bias, establishing when measured responses recover optimal defender decisions without constructing the full payoff matrix. In simulations on 20- and 100-node graphs, empirical ADP rollout costs are within 0.23% and 1.76%, respectively, of exact DP. In a two-dimensional intruder tracking example, both policies reduce network-wide root-mean-square tracking error spread by approximately 25% relative to an unmitigated attack.
item.dc:creator: Nathaniel Mailhot, Mohammad Pirani, Davide Spinello

item.title: A Mixed $H_{\infty}$--Passivity Approach for Leveraging Heat-Pump-Connected District Heating Systems as Frequency Support in Electric Power Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.40955v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Heat-pump (HP)-connected district heating systems (DHSs) can support grid frequency by rapidly modulating HP electrical consumption while accommodating the resulting heat imbalance. Thermal-state-informed HP control improves EPS--DHS coordination, but introduces slower DHS dynamics and heat-side disturbance propagation at the electrical interface on the time scale of secondary frequency control. This paper formulates the regulated DHS as a grid-facing dynamic port and develops a mixed $H_\infty$--passivity framework for disturbance-independent temperature regulation while preserving a clean electrical response during secondary frequency control. Sufficient conditions guarantee local asymptotic stability of the EPS--HP--DHS interconnection across primary frequency control, secondary frequency control, and DHS regulation. These stability conditions are integrated with multi-channel $H_\infty$ attenuation of DHS-state-dependent electrical dynamics, heat-disturbance propagation, and DHS-regulation errors, yielding a tractable convex LMI program for controller synthesis. Cross-model validation deploys controllers synthesized on control-oriented EPS--DHS models, without retuning, on an open-source electromechanical IEEE 39-bus model coupled with four high-fidelity finite-volume DHS models retaining thermal transport, storage, and heat-loss dynamics. The resulting controller improves EPS--DHS coordination without compromising the grid-facing electrical response.
item.dc:creator: Xinyi Yi, Ioannis Lestas

item.title: Learning the Omega-Limit Partition from Approximate Koopman Invariants
item.description: arXiv:2610.40977v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nonlinear dynamical systems with multiple omega-limit sets pose a fundamental challenge for global finite-dimensional Koopman modeling with continuous observables. A natural way to address this challenge is to decompose the state space into forward-invariant regions associated with distinct asymptotic behaviors and to learn a separate Koopman model for each region. This paper studies how to compute such partitions from data. We establish conditions under which Koopman-invariant observables, namely eigenfunctions associated with the unit eigenvalue, characterize the stationary partition induced by omega-limit sets. Building on this characterization, we develop OPAL (Omega-limit Partitions from Approximate invariants Learned from data), an algorithm that extracts partitions from approximate invariant observables. Numerical examples show that the recovered partitions capture the relevant asymptotic regions and support multiple regional linear Koopman models with significantly improved long-horizon prediction capabilities.
item.dc:creator: Dhruv Shah, Jorge Cort\'es

item.title: A Temporal Cellular Sheaf Framework for Multi-Agent Systems with Switching Communication Topologies
item.description: arXiv:2610.40991v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cellular sheaves serve as a natural modeling framework for encoding heterogeneity in the state and interaction spaces of multi-agent systems. This work examines switching communication graphs with the use of temporal cellular sheaves, which we construct to represent heterogeneous agent state spaces, the maps that relate them, and their respective communication constraints. We then develop sufficient conditions under which a multi-agent system defined on a temporal cellular sheaf can solve the target tracking problem by generalizing the existing concept of joint connectivity. Using a Lyapunov-based stability analysis, we demonstrate that the target tracking error of the network converges to a neighborhood of the origin.
item.dc:creator: Brandon Fallin, Wilmer Leal, Austin Copeland, Benjamin Merlin Bumpus, James Fairbanks, Warren E. Dixon

item.title: Optimal climate policy in incomplete electricity markets
item.description: arXiv:2610.41103v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Incomplete long-term contracting in electricity markets can expose investors and consumers to inefficient levels of risk. This paper investigates how incompleteness impacts the optimal choice of climate policy. We develop a game-theoretic model of optimal policy-making in anticipation of how electricity market agents react to a given policy when gas prices and demand are uncertain and contracting is incomplete. In illustrative experiments, we observe that renewable subsidies and carbon prices induce an insurance co-benefit when markets are incomplete. This is because, relative to a complete market benchmark, incompleteness shifts investment from renewables toward gas and exposes consumers to uninsured risk from inter-annual volatility in electricity prices. By incentivizing investment in renewables, subsidies and carbon prices indirectly counteract these distortions. Consequently, incompleteness increases the optimal subsidy and carbon price levels in our experiments. Renewable subsidies exhibit a stronger insurance effect than carbon pricing, as the latter leads to more investment in gas with carbon capture and storage and more volatile electricity prices. While carbon pricing is more economically efficient than subsidies in complete markets, incompleteness shrinks its efficiency advantage and even leads to cases where subsidies are more economically efficient.
item.dc:creator: Emil Dimanchev, Steven A. Gabriel, Stein-Erik Fleten, Filippo Pecci, Magnus Korpas

item.title: Market Efficiency and Capacity Investment under Flexible Price-Making Loads: A Computational Study
item.description: arXiv:2610.41196v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large flexible loads such as data centers can shift consumption across locations and hours to lower their bills. We model a price-making consumer leading the system operator in a Stackelberg game and compare its shifts with a cost-minimizing planner's over a simulated RTS-GMLC year. Strategic temporal and spatial shifting capture 75% and 93% of the planner's savings, forgoing the rest mostly by withholding flexibility to protect favorable prices. Scarce capacity and abundant renewables raise this share for temporal shifting; scarce transmission lowers it for spatial shifting. Temporal and spatial flexibility substitute for thermal and transmission capacity, respectively, and complement renewables.
item.dc:creator: Aron Brenner, Deepjyoti Deka, Saurabh Amin

item.title: EMT Assessment of SCR and X/R Effects on Current-Priority-Dependent LVRT Response of a Grid-Following BESS
item.description: arXiv:2610.41212v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Low-voltage ride-through (LVRT) forces a grid-following inverter to allocate finite converter current between active- and reactive-current objectives. This paper uses a PSCAD electromagnetic-transient (EMT) representation of an aggregated battery energy storage system (BESS) to quantify how short-circuit ratio (SCR) and grid impedance X/R ratio alter that tradeoff. Active-current priority and reactive-current priority are compared for five paired grid conditions under the same 150-ms balanced three-phase fault, with pre-fault active power approximately 0.84 pu, POI reactive-power exchange near 0 pu, and a 1.0-pu dq-current limit. Fundamental positive-sequence voltage and power are reconstructed from 100-$\mu$s three-phase EMT outputs. Across the fixed-fault SCR sweep, the Q-priority late-fault voltage advantage increases from 0.046 pu in the strongest tested grid to 0.129 pu in the weakest; the weakest P-priority case also shows active-power reversal and a pronounced controller-frequency excursion. At fixed SCR, changing X/R produces a smaller increase from 0.092 to 0.112 pu, mainly through reduced P-priority voltage support. Because the common physical fault also deepens the passive retained-voltage condition as SCR decreases, the SCR result is interpreted as a fixed-fault grid-strength sensitivity rather than a constant-sag comparison. Grid strength is the larger sensitivity in the tested matrix, while X/R remains an additional modifier under the studied fault conditions.
item.dc:creator: Dileep Cheerla, Amirthagunaraj Yogarathnam, Divya Jain, Satish Natti

item.title: Control-Layer Interpretation of Reactive Power Recovery Limits in EMT-RMS Model Benchmarking of Inverter-Based Resources
item.description: arXiv:2610.41221v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: EMT--RMS benchmarking is widely used to verify cross-platform consistency of inverter-based resource (IBR) dynamic models. This paper examines a 200 MW anonymized IBR represented in PSCAD and PSS/E. The EMT model separates inverter electrical capability from a plant-level power plant controller (PPC) recovery target, whereas the RMS model represents these functions through REECC and REPCA parameters. Directly assigning the PPC target of $\pm 0.2764$ pu to REPCA hard reactive limits is initialization-inconsistent at the original lagging operating point because the initial reactive command is 0.396273 pu. A second, near-unity-power-factor operating point initializes successfully with the same diagnostic limit, demonstrating that the conflict is operating-point dependent. Using the non-conflicting capability mapping removes the original hard-limit conflict, but the benchmark still shows 18.5--30.2 MVAr post-event POI reactive-power differences from PSCAD. A one-at-a-time REPCA $K_c$ sensitivity under matched benchmark initial conditions further shows that RMS recovery is parameter- and limit-dependent: at $K_c=0.05$ and 0.10 the aggregate machine reactive output reaches the configured capability bounds, while $K_c=0.15$ moves VDOWN, VUP, and HVRT off those bounds and changes their settled POI reactive power by 8.94, 18.00, and 3.17 MVAr, respectively. Machine-to-POI accounting further shows why machine-side saturation need not reproduce the POI-level PPC recovery magnitude. The results distinguish initialization feasibility from recovery equivalence and provide a control-layer diagnostic workflow beyond waveform comparison.
item.dc:creator: Dileep Cheerla, Amirthagunaraj Yogarathnam, Divya Jain, Satish Natti

item.title: Delta-Seeker: Closed-Loop Generative Search for Novel Circuit Design Discovery
item.description: arXiv:2610.41227v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative models are increasingly used for circuit synthesis and optimization by proposing topologies, sizing devices, and exploring large design spaces. We investigate whether they can instead support design discovery, where generated structures must depart from known designs while producing reproducible electrical behavior. We propose Delta-Seeker, a closed-loop circuit search framework that combines discrete diffusion for topology generation and mutation with structural checking, SPICE-in-the-loop sizing, Pareto selection, and feedback from prior search outcomes. The search controller uses progress and recurring structural failures to allocate evaluation effort and steer subsequent topology generation, while independent re-sizing and operating-corner analysis are performed only after search. In generator-only experiments, cross-generation feedback increases structurally valid children from 143 to 945 and reduces the faulty-candidate fraction from 0.925 to 0.761. In op-amp topology discovery at matched sizing cost, Delta-Seeker yields 54 designs that remain feasible in at least three of four independent re-sizings and 18 that additionally pass device-level checks and supply-temperature corner analysis, compared with 38 and 10 under fixed control. Removing cross-generation memory reduces independently robust discoveries from 54 to 43 and seven-corner robust discoveries from 40 to 27. In DC-DC converter search, nearest-parent analysis identifies a corpus-absent topology whose generated switching current path changes its nearest training-corpus parent from infeasible at all four operating corners to feasible at all four, while increasing median efficiency from 31.2% to 98.96%. These results show that closed-loop generative search can support circuit discovery beyond structural novelty by identifying new topologies with independently verified changes in circuit operation.

item.title: Frequency-Calibrated Decision-Focused Learning for BESS Dispatch Under Renewable Uncertainty
item.description: arXiv:2610.41238v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Battery energy storage system (BESS) flexibility depends on state of charge and intertemporal operating constraints. Renewable forecast errors of similar magnitudes can lead to different BESS dispatch results. An error may alter early charging or discharging decisions and reduce the flexibility available for subsequent regulation, while another may have little effect on the resulting schedule. To account for these unequal consequences, this paper proposes Frequency-Calibrated Decision-Focused Learning (FC-DFL), which trains renewable predictors using the realized operating costs of their induced BESS schedules. Gaussian smoothing and solver-based zeroth-order estimation provide training feedback without requiring differentiating through the non-differentiable mixed-integer BESS dispatch problem. The same decision feedback is further combined with prediction sensitivity to develop a decision-oriented XAI method that identifies the input features and forecast periods most consequential to BESS operation. Case studies using German wind and solar data show that FC-DFL reduces the integrated absolute frequency-deviation metric by 6.05% and decision regret by 23.92% relative to accuracy-based predict-then-optimize method. The XAI analysis further demonstrates that the identified high-impact forecast periods produce 2.84 times larger average absolute changes in realized operating cost than low-impact periods. These findings highlight the importance of incorporating downstream decision-making outcomes into renewable forecasting and demonstrate the value of FC-DFL in improving BESS regulation and providing operationally meaningful forecast explanations.
item.dc:creator: Zihan Meng, Chenxi Hu, Xin Cui, Francis Yunhe Hou

item.title: Multi-Timescale Deliverability of Shared Hybrid Storage for AI Data Center Campuses
item.description: arXiv:2610.41249v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial intelligence data center (AIDC) campuses contain sustained power variations and subsecond power fluctuations, requiring both sufficient stored energy and fast response. A shared hybrid energy storage system (HESS) can mitigate aggregate AIDC power deviations, but interval-based schedules cannot capture the delay between commanded and delivered power at the campus point of common coupling (PCC). To this end, this paper proposes a multi-timescale scheduling model for mitigating AIDC power fluctuations with the shared HESS. First, it models electrical pooling at the campus bus and constrains the shared HESS to a single PCC injection. Second, a two-layer model passes five-minute scheduled power, energy state, and reserve capacity to a causal fast response model that distinguishes commanded power from delivered power. Case studies using the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) GenAI Power Profiles Dataset show reductions in both PCC and fast integral absolute error (IAE), while retaining most of the improvement available under ideal response.
item.dc:creator: Zihan Meng, Ruizhang Yang, Chenxi Hu, Francis Yunhe Hou

item.title: Control-Oriented Modeling of Heat Exchangers with Improved Low-Flow Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.41364v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing low-order models of heat exchangers can lose dynamic accuracy at low flow rates, when fluid residence times become significant. This paper proposes two control-oriented models that improve the low-flow performance. The first extends a finite-volume formulation with the first spatial temperature moment, whereas the second uses Chebyshev--Lobatto collocation. Both capture the coupled heat-transfer and transport dynamics and improve the performance when the system behavior is dominated by the inlet-temperature dynamics. At equal state dimension, comparisons with a high-order reference show more accurate delayed outlet-temperature responses while retaining steady-state accuracy.
item.dc:creator: Noah Hofmann, Stefan L. H\"olzl, Robert Bauer, Martin Steinberger

item.title: Riemannian Optimization on Unknown Manifolds via Stochastic Proximal Refinement
item.description: arXiv:2610.41379v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study Riemannian optimization on an unknown manifold accessed only through feasible samples. The central challenge is to turn feasible samples into optimization steps, i.e., the samples are drawn from the unknown feasible manifold, but do not directly provide the tangent spaces, projections, or retractions required by classic Riemannian methods. Moreover, regions with low objective values may be sparsely represented in the data, so directly sampling from a distribution fitted to these observations can require many draws to find better feasible solutions. We introduce Proximal Refinement on Implicit Smooth Manifolds (PRISM), which turns feasible-sample access into an iterative optimization procedure by repeatedly sampling an objective-aware proximal distribution conditioned on the current iterate. Theoretically, we show that PRISM recovers the effect of Riemannian-gradient refinement, leading to provable objective descent, feasibility (manifold adherence), and convergence toward first-order stationarity. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through synthetic experiments illustrating its geometric properties and applications to data-driven building control and diverse real world optimization tasks, highlighting its potential as a general framework for data-driven optimization across scientific and engineering domains.
item.dc:creator: Ruixiang Wu, Jiahao Ai, Tinko Sebastian Bartels, Xuanzhuo Liu, Yifei Wu, Yu Mao, Tongxin Li, Costas Courcoubetis

item.title: Koopman Greedy Spiking Control for Nonlinear Systems under Firing-Rate Limits
item.description: arXiv:2610.41530v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neuromorphic controllers interact with physical systems through fixed-amplitude spikes whose timing conveys control information. Existing Lyapunov-based greedy spiking controllers guarantee stability but are restricted to linear systems and neglect firing-rate limits. We extend greedy spiking control to nonlinear systems using Koopman operator theory. For observable dictionaries invariant under differentiation along the input direction, spike-induced state translations admit an exact linear representation in lifted coordinates, enabling exact modeling of spiking jump dynamics. This allows firing decisions to be formulated as comparisons of quadratic Lyapunov functions in the lifted space. We prove practical stability of a clocked, rate-limited controller with an explicit ultimate bound and develop a data-driven design based on Koopman eigenfunctions learned from unforced data by generator-based regression. The weights of the Lyapunov function are synthesized by a linear program that enforces a sampled relaxation of the rate-limited control-Lyapunov condition. Applied to an inverted pendulum, the learned eigenfunctions recover the system energy, and the proposed controller achieves swing-up and stabilization from nearly all initial conditions despite severe actuation limits.
item.dc:creator: Nader Meskin

item.title: Report on Stability Analysis of Islanded Power Systems with Grid-Forming Converters
item.description: arXiv:2610.41538v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Islanded power systems are inherently challenging to operate due to limited interconnection, low inertia, and weak short-circuit strength. As renewable and inverter-based resources replace synchronous machines, these challenges worsen, causing faster frequency deviations, greater voltage volatility, and higher risk of instability. This report summarizes the differences between islanded and interconnected systems and reviews key stability issues in islanded grids: frequency stability, converter-driven interactions, voltage stability, large-disturbance behavior, and small-signal dynamics. Grid-forming (GFM) voltage source converters are a promising solution because they can establish voltage and frequency, emulate synchronous machine behavior, and provide grid strength, virtual inertia, fast frequency response, voltage regulation, and black-start capability. The report examines relevant GFM control strategies and evaluates their capabilities in weak, low-inertia islanded grids. Challenges remain, particularly interoperability, control coordination among multiple inverter-based resources, lack of standardized grid code requirements, and coordination of protection devices. Successful deployment requires advances in interoperability, harmonized grid codes, and grid planning that considers the unique features of islanded systems, along with clear GFM functionality requirements. Finally, a case study illustrates the stability-enhancing capability of GFM converters in weak grids through small-signal stability analysis. Overall, GFM technology is a key enabler of reliable, renewable-dominant island power systems, but broader adoption depends on continued technical and regulatory development.
item.dc:creator: Anup Joshi, Luis A. Garcia-Reyes, Qingyuan Gong, Xavier Guillaud, Javier Renedo, Dirk Van Hertem

item.title: Channel Measurement and Characteristics Analysis for Indoor Flexible Pinching Antenna Systems in the mmWave Band
item.description: arXiv:2610.41567v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pinching antenna (PA) systems offer flexible antenna configurations for future wireless communications, yet how PA geometry, orientation, and position affect channel characteristics in practical environments remains insufficiently studied. To address this gap, this paper first presents an indoor PA system channel measurement campaign at 59.5~GHz. A dedicated time-domain channel sounder is developed with frequency conversion and a circular-waveguide-to-dielectric-waveguide transition to feed the radio frequency (RF) signal into a flexible dielectric waveguide. Using this platform, office measurements quantify channel attenuation and channel characteristics by examining four PA geometries, arc PA orientation, circle PA pinching position, and transmitter--receiver height difference. The channel measurement data are analyzed in terms of path loss, shadow fading, root-mean-square (RMS) delay spread, Rician K-factor, normalized capacity, and spatial similarity. Indoor path loss models for PA systems are fitted for each PA geometry. The results reveal geometry-dependent attenuation and shadow-fading variability, with the arc PA showing greater variability than the circle PA. Arc PA rotation shifts the delay spread and conditional K-factor distributions. Moving the circle PA produces nonmonotonic changes in delay spread and normalized capacity, while spatial similarity remains relatively high at many receiver locations as the pinching position changes. These observations provide an empirical basis for PA systems channel model and system design.
item.dc:creator: Haoyang Li, Weidong Liu, Songjiang Yang, Zhensheng Chen, Jing Zhu, Gaojie Chen, Wei Huang

item.title: Probability-Layer Clustering for Bound-and-Budget Calibration in Multi-Bound Robust Bidding of Renewable-Based Virtual Power Plants
item.description: arXiv:2610.41633v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: RVPPs that aggregate dispatchable and non-dispatchable renewable energy sources, storage, and flexible demand that bid in the day-ahead and secondary reserve markets must cope with uncertainties in market prices, renewable generation, and demand. MBRO is well suited to this setting because it hedges adverse realizations through several deviation layers while keeping the final bidding problem as a tractable, scenario-free MILP. Its performance, however, depends on how the deviation bounds and uncertainty budgets are calibrated. Existing MBRO implementations commonly rely on fixed percentile-based bounds and externally specified budget vectors, usually examined through sensitivity analysis. This paper proposes PL-MBRO, that constructs parameter-specific deviation bounds from historical data conditional on selected risk-attitude quantiles and automatically derives the corresponding uncertainty budgets from empirical cluster probabilities. For each uncertain parameter, k-medians clustering partitions the historical daily profiles into representative probability layers; the cluster median defines the balanced representative, while favorable and adverse within-cluster percentiles define the optimistic and pessimistic representatives. The empirical cluster probabilities are mapped to integer full-horizon uncertainty budgets over the 96 quarter-hourly periods, while the robust inner problem determines the periods in which the corresponding deviation layers are most adverse to the schedule. Compared with a percentilebased MBRO benchmark, in-sample and out-of-sample tests on an RVPP bidding in both markets show that PL-MBRO consistently achieves better realized economic outcomes across the optimistic, balanced, and pessimistic strategies, with improvements of up to 92.7% in-sample and 57.3% out-of-sample, measured relative to the absolute value of the corresponding benchmark realized profit.
item.dc:creator: Hadi Nemati, \'Alvaro Ortega, Enrique Lobato, Luis Rouco

item.title: Scaly: an Optimizing Compiler for Optimal Control
item.description: arXiv:2610.41762v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present Scaly, an open-source optimizing compiler for optimal control, written in Python, that generates fast C code. Scaly provides a modeling language embedded in Python for the parametric optimization problems that arise in model predictive control and moving horizon estimation, and computes the sparse derivatives that standard optimization solvers need. Scaly accepts general nonlinear programs but applies optimizations specific to optimal control, which preserve the repeated structure of a problem, such as the stages of a horizon, through differentiation down to the generated loops. The generated C depends only on the C math library and never allocates memory dynamically. On three benchmark problems, Scaly evaluates the Hessian of the Lagrangian up to 26 times faster than CasADi, with smaller binaries and build times that stay nearly constant with the horizon. With the same solver, Scaly shortens the solver time per control step on every benchmark, by a factor of up to 9.
item.dc:creator: Tudor A. Oancea, Colin N. Jones

item.title: Safe Planning for Black-Box Systems via MAP Inference with Truncated Diffusion Priors and CBF-Informed Gibbs Likelihoods
item.description: arXiv:2610.41873v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper proposes a maximum a posteriori (MAP) inference framework with a truncated diffusion prior for safe planning (TDP-SafeMAP). Under a generalized Bayesian formulation, a criterion based on covariance condition number determines the reverse diffusion truncation timestep, and the clean control distribution predicted at that timestep is approximated by a Gaussian prior encoding the control regularities and uncertainty of expert data. An energy function containing a control barrier function (CBF) constraint violation measure defines a Gibbs task likelihood that incorporates physical constraint information. After fusing the prior and likelihood, the covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy (CMA-ES), whose core update admits an interpretation as a sampling-based approximation to natural-gradient ascent, approximates the posterior mode using only black-box evaluations. B\'ezier-curve-based dimensionality reduction and related techniques further improve computational efficiency and task-completion capability. Theoretical analysis establishes an error bound for the approximate MAP solution, an explicit condition for CBF safety preservation, and the equivalence of the MAP problem under prior whitening. Experimental results show that the proposed framework consistently generates safe, smooth, and goal-reaching trajectories, providing an effective and practical statistical inference approach to safe planning for black-box systems.
item.dc:creator: Shanghan Liu, Jitao Sun, Junhui Zhang

item.title: Preference-Conditioned Group-Relative Policy Optimization for Terminally Constrained Multi-Objective Control
item.description: arXiv:2610.41884v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-objective optimal control is commonly addressed by reinforcement learning with fixed scalarization weights, requiring a separate training run and constraint enforcement for each trade-off. This letter extends critic-free group-relative policy optimization to terminally constrained multi-objective control: a single preference-conditioned policy is trained over random preferences and returns a feasible approximation of the Pareto front in one run. Three structural results are established. Group normalization after scalarization preserves the prescribed preference, whereas per-objective normalization induces policy-dependent distortion; with pairwise distinct normalization scales, only single-objective preferences remain unchanged. A positive floor prevents the terminal-constraint multiplier from vanishing and renders the penalty exact when the floor exceeds a geometric multiplier. Deterministic terminal violation is bounded by expected stochastic violation plus a term depending on terminal-state curvature and action variance, so stochastic feasibility alone does not certify deterministic execution. On a heavy-duty range-extender powertrain with six stage costs and a terminal state-of-charge band, a representative training run places all 32 preference-grid solutions in band on six cycles inside and outside the training pool. Averaged over ten runs, the method yields more in-band solutions under deterministic execution than a critic-based conditioned baseline with the same terminal-constraint handling.
item.dc:creator: Md Ragib Rownak, Sidra Ghayour Bhatti, Qadeer Ahmed

item.title: Safety Verification for Voltage Control in Inverter Dominated Radial Distribution Networks under Actuator and Sensor Adversarial Attacks
item.description: arXiv:2610.41910v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper develops a safety verification framework for inverter-based radial distribution networks under sensor and actuator attacks. Each customer is equipped with a droop-based controller to regulate its voltage within a desirable bound of a reference, i.e., to achieve safety. In our setting, attacks and disturbances enter the droop-based controllers, while actuator attacks corrupt the reactive power injected into the network. Consequently, invariance of the controller state alone does not guarantee compliance with inverter capacities or customer voltage limits. To address this challenge, we derive conditions to guarantee that the reactive power state remains inside a predefined ellipsoid, while at the same time ensuring that the attacked reactive power injections and customer voltages respect predetermined operating limits that hold uniformly for the entire predefined ellipsoid. Together, these conditions guarantee safety under all admissible disturbances and state-dependent sensor and actuator attacks. Finally, we express the resulting containment condition as a linear matrix inequality (LMI) feasibility problem. A five-customer radial network based on the CIGRE benchmark corroborates our theoretical developments in simulations.
item.dc:creator: Georgios Pantazis, Revi Boelen, Michelle S. Chong

item.title: Epidemic Forecasting and Behavioral Response Estimation with a Behavior-Coupled SEIR Model
item.description: arXiv:2610.41943v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic has exhibited multiple waves of infections, reflecting feedback between disease transmission and adaptive population behavior. Accurately predicting and understanding these dynamics remains a central challenge for epidemic modeling. In this paper, we develop a forecasting framework based on a Susceptible-Exposed-Infectious-Recovered (SEIR) model coupled with an evolutionary model of behavioral adaptation, in which population compliance with protective measures evolves in response to perceived infection risk and associated costs. We formulate forecasting as the estimation of behavioral incentive parameters that govern the coupled behavior-disease dynamics, using hospitalization time series data together with standard assumptions on disease-related parameters. Using the inferred parameters, we generate rolling monthly forecasts of infection levels and evaluate the approach on both synthetic data and hospitalization time series from multiple U.S. states (Texas, California, Colorado, and Arizona). The proposed framework provides a principled way to incorporate behavior-disease feedback into epidemic forecasting while yielding interpretable estimates of population-level incentives.
item.dc:creator: Sungi Hong, Soham Das, Hossein Khazaei, Alfredo Garcia, Keith Paarporn, Ceyhun Eksin

item.title: Risk Assessment of Fair Multi-Period Dynamic Operating Envelopes under Uncertainty
item.description: arXiv:2610.42014v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dynamic operating envelopes (DOEs) can allocate time-varying export capacity to distributed energy resources (DERs), and while they are not intended to make operations immune to voltage violations, they should guide operations to mostly remain inside expected values under changing regimes and residual forecast errors. However, although recent literature proposed many different techniques for implementing DOEs, there is sparse discussion of analyzing and quantifying the risk of using more or less conservative DOEs under uncertain operating regimes. Having this gap in mind, this paper develops a risk-oriented extension of a previously established fair distributed multi-period optimal power flow (OPF) framework, where fair or technical DOEs are fixed as first-stage decisions and the OPF leverages battery energy storage and renewable curtailment as recourse under regime uncertainties. An independent nonlinear AC power flow then computes a resulting ensemble, which is summarized by (i) voltage-violation probability, severity, and a persistence metric for consecutive out-of-band hours, (ii) curtailment and Jain and Gini indices, and (iii) model deviations. Different probability situations are assessed, ranging from uniform, sunny-heavy, night-peak-heavy, and adversarial, which separate the envelope design from the assumed operating distribution. An optional outer loop allows for fine-tuning a fairness--efficiency parameter under explicit violation and persistence budgets. The combination of the outer loop and the overall framework, which quantifies how often and how severely operating limits are exceeded, creates an auditable methodology mixing equitable export allocation, distributed recourse, and AC risk assessment for active distribution network operators, and this framework is assessed using up to 1000 Monte Carlo scenarios per mixture and DOE design.
item.dc:creator: Pedro Salom\~ao Quessongo, Daniel Gebbran, Wilhiam de Carvalho, Clodomiro Unsihuay-Vila

item.title: A Neural Network Approach towards Real-Time Knot Point Density Estimates for the Nonlinear Quadrotor
item.description: arXiv:2610.42027v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spline representations provide a compact way to approximate continuous trajectories using a finite number of parameters. When approximating trajectories generated by dynamical systems, the efficiency of a spline representation depends strongly on the placement of knot points. Uniform knot distributions often lead to inefficient representations, requiring either unnecessary control points or producing poor approximations in regions where the trajectory varies rapidly. In this work we propose a learning-based method for adaptive knot placement in B-spline approximations of trajectories generated by ordinary differential equations. A neural network learns a mapping from the initial condition of the system to quantities that characterize the local variation of the resulting trajectory. These estimates are used to construct nonuniform knot distributions that approximately equidistribute a local error indicator, reducing the number of control points needed to meet a prescribed accuracy.
item.dc:creator: Jasmine Ratchford, Raffaele Romagnoli, Mark H. Klein

item.title: System-Level Factors Influencing AGC Cyber-Attack Success and RAS Vulnerability in Multi-Area Grids
item.description: arXiv:2610.42047v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automatic generation control (AGC) stabilizes frequency and scheduled power exchanges among interconnected areas, yet its reliance on communication networks introduces cyber-vulnerabilities. This work examines coordinated AGC cyber-attacks in the presence of remedial action schemes (RAS) and identifies operating conditions under which an attacker can drive grid frequency beyond safe limits while evading RAS. A feedback-based attack policy is used to manipulate AGC signals and steer system frequency toward unsafe trajectories. Then, a large nested-loop parametric sweep---spanning attacked-area inertia relative to its interconnected neighboring area, AGC capacity versus maximum tie-line transfer, AGC update rate, load damping, and bi-directional power transfers---generates over 1.45 million scenarios. These are classified using a decision tree to establish guidelines to distinguish successful from unsuccessful attacks based on frequency deviations. The resulting vulnerability guidelines are validated on a three-area system using phasor-domain simulations with IEEE 9-bus area models, detailed turbine--governor dynamics, and under/over-frequency load and generation shedding. Results show that specific combinations of AGC capacity, inertia distribution, and pre-attack tie-line loading increase the likelihood of successful attacks, offering operators actionable criteria for identifying vulnerable operating conditions.
item.dc:creator: Abdulmannan Ajabnoor, Zhi Jin Zhang, Maryam Saeedifard, Dominic Gro{\ss}

item.title: Measurement-Based Assessment of Decadal Inertia and Primary Frequency Response Trends in the US Eastern Interconnection
item.description: arXiv:2610.42073v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Changes in the generation mix of the U.S. Eastern Interconnection (EI) raise questions about long-term frequency performance, particularly inertia and primary frequency response (PFR). This paper jointly examines these characteristics using synchronized FNET/GridEye frequency measurements and confirmed generation-trip events from 2013 to 2025. A representative EI frequency trajectory is constructed using the median of geographically distributed measurements. Effective inertia is estimated quarterly from the early post-disturbance rate of change of frequency (RoCoF), using a 3-second window and least-squares fitting. PFR is evaluated using the beta metric, which measures aggregate frequency response from disturbance size and the A-to-B frequency deviation. Annual beta estimates are obtained after filtering events by starting frequency and disturbance size to improve comparability across years. Results show that EI effective inertia varies seasonally and follows a non-monotonic trend rather than a uniform long-term decline. Over the same period, coal generation decreased while natural gas, wind, and solar generation increased. Changes in synchronous generator commitment and operating conditions may have offset some expected inertia reductions. Filtered beta generally increased from the mid-2010s to the early 2020s, with year-to-year variability thereafter. The different trends show that early inertial behavior and broader aggregate frequency response have not evolved in parallel. Joint analysis of inertia and beta offers a more complete measurement-based assessment of EI frequency performance during the generation transition.
item.dc:creator: Saurav Dulal, Mark Baldwin, Narges Ghiasi, Mohammed Olama, Ali R. Ekti, Nils M. Stenvig, Yilu Liu

item.title: From Teleoperation to Long-Horizon Dexterity: Evaluating Visuomotor Skills and Offline Proxies for Dexterous Manipulation
item.description: arXiv:2610.40828v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Imitation learning policies are intended to make robotic manipulation robust to variations in object pose, appearance, and environment that challenge pre-programmed motion. However, real-world performance remains difficult to predict, as conventional optimization signals such as validation loss show no consistent relationship with robot success. To identify the design choices that govern real-world performance, 281 imitation-learning policies spanning seven policy families were evaluated in approximately 1,700 real-robot trials of RJ45 connector grasping and insertion using a five-fingered robotic hand. Controlled ablations showed that observation and action representations dominated conventional optimizer and sampling choices. For point-cloud policies, region-of-interest cropping, representation in the robot-base frame, and normalization within the point encoder each improved success by 70-100 percentage points. For the vision-language-action policy, absolute rather than relative action prediction improved insertion success by up to 70 percentage points. Skill decomposition, multi-view perception, and recovery demonstrations were associated with the strongest-performing systems, although their effects were not independently isolated. Of 67 offline metrics evaluated, only five measures of predicted-motion smoothness and directness reliably correlated with insertion success (r = -0.70 to -0.80), and only within a single policy family. These results identify representation choices as key determinants of real-world imitation-learning performance and show that offline metrics can shortlist policies, but cannot replace real-robot evaluation.
item.dc:creator: Ammar N. Abbas, Aayush Jain, Prashanth Viswanath, Nivesh Gadipudi, Giulia Vilone, Jim Gibbons

item.title: How a group that cannot communicate knows itself by its enemy
item.description: arXiv:2610.40835v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Teams that cannot communicate seem stuck with what each member sees. We show that their opponent can tell them the rest. Silent hunters, jammed robots and traders who never meet all face an adversary that reacts to the group as a whole; every member can read that reaction, a tell, and learn what no member knows alone. One tell can do the work of a message from every member. The adversary would rather hide, but hiding interferes with its own task, and a team that commits in advance to how it will respond decides how much hiding is worth. A committed team never loses when its opponent cares more about its own goals, and does as well as a fully informed team exactly when the opponent's stake outweighs any gain from lying. Below that point the team learns more by trusting less: in a solved Gaussian model it obtains the truth by promising not to use all of it and keeps the cost the opponent would have paid to conceal; an exact test decides when this holds in finite games. How a team spreads its trust matters too. A lone uninformed member with a full-support prior needs a private coin, but with additive squared-error losses two interchangeable members who respond differently replace it, and a small discount on trust insures against misjudging the enemy. Information, on this view, is not only gathered or aggregated; it is produced by how a team commits to respond.
item.dc:creator: Gregory Falco

item.title: Addendum to "Optimal Steering of a Linear Stochastic System to a Final Probability Distribution, Part II"
item.description: arXiv:2610.40888v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We hereby fill in a gap in an induction argument used in the proof of a theorem on state-covariance controllability of linear stochastic systems in an earlier paper by the authors. The mathematical statement is true. The missing point in the proof concerns the assertion that, in the canonical single-input case, the control can be assigned arbitrary endpoint values. We amend the argument by proving a slightly stronger induction statement that permits arbitrary finite endpoint jets of the control. An independent approach to homogeneous state-covariance controllability was provided in a paper by Abdelgalil and Georgiou (2025) as a corollary of strong controllability results on $\GLp(n,\mathbb R)$, and shown herein that it extends to the case of additive noise as well.
item.dc:creator: Yongxin Chen, Tryphon T. Georgiou, Michele Pavon

item.title: Incremental Stability of Gradient Flows under Generalized Polyak-{\L}ojasiewicz Inequalities and Its Implications for General Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.40897v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Gradient flows of twice continuously differentiable strongly convex and convex objectives are, respectively, incrementally exponentially stable and non-expansive in the Euclidean metric. In this work, we investigate to what extent these properties extend to nonconvex objectives satisfying generalized Polyak-{\L}ojasiewicz inequalities. For objectives with a unique minimizer, we establish conditions under which the gradient flow is contracting in a state-dependent Riemannian metric and incrementally exponentially stable. For objectives with nonunique minimizers, we generalize the non-expansivity of convex objectives to incremental stability for more general nonconvex objectives. We focus on incremental stability due to its implication to convergence to equilibrium points; when paired with a Lyapunov function it implies pointwise convergence to a minimizer and continuity of the endpoint map. Along the way, we derive new structural results for incrementally stable nonlinear systems and extend the analysis to Heavy-Ball and Dynamical Inertial Newton flows.
item.dc:creator: Andreas Oliveira, Arthur C. B. de Oliveira, Mario Sznaier, Eduardo Sontag

item.title: Fast and Accurate Hydro Unit Commitment
item.description: arXiv:2610.40918v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce a fast novel algorithm to commit hydro-generators. We show that our algorithm can commit 56 generators for 200 days 10,000 times faster than Hexaly, the leading commercial solver for scheduling problems, without sacrificing solution quality. Our method can commit 1792 generators for an entire year in approximately 20 seconds on commodity hardware. Hexaly is unable to solve problems of this size in reasonable time. We attain this runtime improvement by introducing a greedy-heuristic tailored for hydro units. We provide a direction for a possible proof that the error our solver makes decreases with the problem size. This is supported by our experimental results. We prove that our solver's runtime scales log-linearly in the number of generators and time periods.
item.dc:creator: Shaked Regev, Evan J. R. Brody

item.title: Confidence-Modulated Safety Filtering for End-to-End Policies
item.description: arXiv:2610.40922v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: End-to-end policies, from task-specific controllers to robot foundation models, learn complex behavior from raw observations but are not guaranteed to remain safe, so they are often wrapped in a safety filter. The resulting system operates under two domains: the filter's operational design domain (ODD), where its assumptions hold and safety is certified, and the policy's competence domain, where it is reliable. Filters typically fix their conservativeness regardless of the policy's competence, trading performance inside the ODD against margin beyond it. We ask whether the policy's confidence should set that level, and propose a filter-agnostic pipeline that modulates it at runtime: inside the ODD, where every setting is safe, confidence buys performance; beyond it, low confidence adds margin, which helps when it flags where the filter's model fails. Preliminary F1TENTH simulations, where this holds, show the modulated filter combining the strengths of permissive and conservative filters.
item.dc:creator: Javier Borquez, Jaime F. Fisac

item.title: Learning Stabilizing Latent Feedback Controllers via Multi-Step Backward Losses
item.description: arXiv:2610.40931v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Can learned latent dynamics models support the design of feedback controllers that provably stabilize the original system? For linear time-invariant systems, we show that learning linear autoencoders and latent dynamics with multi-step prediction-reconstruction losses $\unicode{x2014}$ which we term "backward losses" as they encourage latent trajectories to reconstruct full state trajectories $\unicode{x2014}$ provably recovers the structure needed for stabilization. Specifically, a sufficiently long reconstruction horizon ensures that a minimum ${H}_\infty$-norm controller designed using the learned latent model stabilizes the original system through output-feedback via the corresponding encoder, provided the latent dimension is large enough to capture all non-stable modes of the underlying system. We also show why both reconstruction and a multi-step horizon are essential: forward prediction losses that require only low prediction error along latent trajectories admit global loss minimizers that discard unstable modes regardless of horizon length, while single-step reconstruction losses can yield latent models whose stabilizing controllers fail to stabilize the original system. Finally, experiments on a non-linear flexible-arm system illustrate the practical implications of our results for learning non-linear autoencoders and latent dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Paul Lutkus, Lars Lindemann, Stephen Tu

item.title: Temporal and spatial couplings in the dynamics of human walking and running
item.description: arXiv:2610.40948v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Rhythmic behaviours such as walking and running are commonly modelled as dynamical systems around a stable limit cycle. To keep such models tractable, it is usually assumed that each step depends only on the previous one, that the limit cycle is fixed, and that the sagittal and frontal planes can be studied separately. Here, we test these assumptions in seven public datasets of human gait (71 participants), including 16 people who both walked and ran. We fit linear step-to-step maps and validate them by cross-validation, holding out more data where more data exist. At first sight, gait has memory: the state two steps back lowers the prediction error by up to 29\%. Yet most of this temporal coupling vanishes once the operating point may drift slowly and measurement noise is modelled; gait remains limit-cycle-like, around an operating point that moves. Running keeps more memory than walking in the same people. Spatial coupling between the planes is present in most participants, mainly from sagittal to frontal, but weak. This supports planar models of healthy gait, while a repeatable, task-dependent coupling index may serve as a measure of gait quality. The simple models are wrong, but useful enough.
item.dc:creator: Mustafa Mert Ankarali

item.title: RC Prediction: A Python Package for Parameter-Aware Reservoir Computing
item.description: arXiv:2610.40984v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A nonlinear dynamical system can be characterized by the autonomous evolution of its state in time and its dependence on system parameters. As a parameter varies, the dynamics can change quantitatively and, at bifurcation points, qualitatively. When the governing equations are unknown, a data-driven model should therefore capture both elements from observational data, rather than reproduce the dynamics at a single operating condition only. Parameter-aware reservoir computing (PARC) is a model-free framework for this purpose, where the parameter is supplied to a reservoir computer through an additional input channel. PARC is trained on time series recorded at several parameter values, and the trained reservoir, run in closed loop as an autonomous dynamical system, generates trajectories at parameter values that were never observed. rc_prediction is an open-source Python package that implements this workflow. It provides multi-parameter training of a reservoir, autonomous closed-loop prediction at user-specified parameter values, parameter scans, and a standard echo state network for forecasting at a fixed parameter. Hyperparameter optimization and optional GPU acceleration through PyTorch are also provided. We use three benchmark dynamical systems as examples to demonstrate its usage. As one of the featured applications, here we illustrate the prediction of critical transitions and system collapse: trained only on pre-critical data, the model is queried beyond the training range to predict whether the system collapses, to estimate the critical parameter $p_c^{*}$, and to characterize transient lifetimes.
item.dc:creator: Jin-Cheng Rao, Zheng-Meng Zhai, Ying-Cheng Lai

item.title: A Robust Approach to Belief Mismatch in Non-cooperative Dynamic Games
item.description: arXiv:2610.40999v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Game-theoretic models are increasingly used to describe multi-agent interactions in control and robotics applications. However, theoretical and computational complexity makes these models intractable in many dynamic, incomplete information scenarios. Recent work makes strong assumptions to reduce computational complexity: agents share sensor measurements with one another and maintain a common estimate of state uncertainty. Unfortunately, these assumptions enforce a degree of cooperation in generically noncooperative interactions. This paper takes the perspective of an ego agent seeking both computational tractability and robustness to unanticipated behavior of other agents due to mismatched state estimates from private---rather than shared---sensor measurements. To that end, we formulate the game theoretic planning problem in an augmented belief space with perturbed Bayesian dynamics that allows the ego to predict all agents' potentially divergent state estimates. These perturbations are chosen by a hypothetical adversary, ``nature,'' to reflect how non-ego agents' state estimates---based on measurements the ego agent will not see at runtime---may deviate from the ego's own belief. Ultimately, our approach can be understood in the spirit of classical H-infinity robust control, extended to noncooperative, stochastic dynamic games. We present a solver with polynomial-time iterations and conduct two experiments which show how robust belief space reasoning leads ego agents to proactively limit their future vulnerability to model misspecification of other agents' beliefs and actions, reducing performance degradation by over 48%.
item.dc:creator: Ryan Park, Li-huan Shen, Jesse Milzman, Negar Mehr, David Fridovich-Keil

item.title: Koopman--Lyapunov and Koopman--Riccati Controller Synthesis
item.description: arXiv:2610.41141v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While the Koopman operator-based lifted representations of nonlinear autonomous and controlled systems have been well covered in the literature, the direct controller synthesis problem largely remains open. As the controlled system is generally a bilinear (instead of fully linear) Koopman model, controller synthesis appears to lose the linear--quadratic structures of the classical Lyapunov and Riccati methods for finite-dimensional linear systems. However, in infinite dimensions, bilinearity in the feature map should be merely artifactual and hence reducible to linearity in principle. In this work, by considering the operator semigroups in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space with a linear--Sobolev kernel and utilizing the Yosida approximation of their generators, the synthesis problems of a stabilizing controller and an input-unconstrained optimal controller can be formulated as an operator Lyapunov inequality and an operator Riccati equation, respectively. These formulations recover the desirable linear--quadratic structures, and hence, with sample data, they are solvable efficiently in analogous ways to usual linear systems by semidefinite programming solvers and Kleinman iterations, respectively. In addition to proving control performance bounds dependent on the sampling denseness and Yosida regularization, through numerical comparison to linearized LQR, bilinear EDMD-based synthesis, nonlinear MPC, and Koopman MPC methods on numerical models and process control examples, this work demonstrates the proposed Koopman--Riccati synthesis as a computationally efficient approach to obtain a near-optimal state-feedback control law.
item.dc:creator: Wentao Tang

item.title: DistFlow and Its Conic Relaxation: Regularity, Monotonicity, and Hybrid Exactness via Graph Decomposition
item.description: arXiv:2610.41220v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Classical exactness conditions for conic relaxations of the DistFlow model rely, among other assumptions, either on all nodal injections being adjustable or on a network-wide path condition. In practice, these conditions may not hold uniformly across a feeder: controllable distributed energy resources (DERs) sit at some buses and fixed loads at others, while reverse flows from DER-rich regions can violate the path condition. This paper certifies exactness region by region and composes the regional certificates, accounting for perturbations that propagate downstream through voltages. We first introduce a subtree voltage stability region, in which the network and all compatible subtrees remain regular. Within it, two endpoint sign conditions, one relaxing the nonnegative-flow assumption and one implied by the classical path condition, yield monotone responses of voltages, currents, and losses to root voltages. Using duality, the implicit function theorem, and sign properties of inverse sensitivity matrices, we recast both classical arguments as individual sign certificates on branch multipliers. This turns exactness into a branchwise property that can be certified region by region. A partition rule then splits the network into dispatchable and passive subtrees, and a hybrid certificate combines their local conditions into exactness of the full-network relaxation, under additional operating-limit and objective conditions. In particular, placing controllable DERs at both ends of a branch with large reverse flow exempts that branch from the passive sign conditions.
item.dc:creator: Xinliang Dai

item.title: HIPC: Humanoid Iterative Planning and Control via Goal-Conditioned Motion Closure
item.description: arXiv:2610.41334v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent generative models are widely used to provide whole-body motion for humanoid tracking. Current methods combine motion generators with controllers in an open-loop paradigm, which leads to critical issues: tracking errors can accumulate into spatial drift, and the planner cannot adapt to unexpected physical disturbances without feedback from physical execution. However, directly feeding realized states back to the planner in a closed loop can cause discontinuities, resulting in physical jitter and even falls, since such states are out of distribution during training. To bridge this gap, we propose HIPC, a real-time Humanoid Iterative Planning and Control framework that couples a generative model with motion tracking into a unified planning-and-control paradigm. HIPC introduces a goal-conditioned motion planning trained with a canonical motion representation that avoids gimbal-lock singularities under extreme orientations and supports motion generation on diverse geometric and semantic conditions. Then, HIPC adopts two strategies, deviation-decayed recovery and history re-anchoring, to mitigate the out-of-distribution shift caused by realized-state feedback. Finally, HIPC operates a real-time asynchronous planning-and-control system, with latency compensation to reduce temporal mismatch for inference delay. Extensive experiments confirm the effectiveness of HIPC under switching and composition of diverse conditions. Results show that HIPC achieves state-of-the-art goal-reaching accuracy among existing methods while simultaneously demonstrating robustness to physical perturbations and the ability to recover from falls.
item.dc:creator: Yi Han, Xingyu Chen, Zixuan Lang, Qianyang Wu, Yuhang Lin, Ji Ma, Liang Li, Dongting Li, Xinpeng Liu, Ruoli Dai, Hesheng Wang, Renjing Xu, Lei Han

item.title: Quantile Propagation Planning for Budgeted Tail-Risk Evaluation
item.description: arXiv:2610.41351v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Risk-aware planning must identify rare, costly outcomes using only a limited number of model evaluations. Monte Carlo rollouts spend this budget on noisy tail estimates, while planning from the mean can miss the tail entirely. We introduce quantile propagation planning (QPP), which propagates a small, fixed set of disturbance quantiles through the dynamics and integrates the resulting cost curve to evaluate both mean and tail risk. The method is exact at the propagated levels, converges as the quantile grid is refined, and admits a one-sided conservatism guarantee under stated structural conditions. In controlled overload and inventory tasks, QPP reduces realized tail cost and constraint violations relative to mean-rollout planning. On overload, it remains competitive with sampled evaluators that use substantially more trajectories. These results position QPP as a transparent, budget-controlled approach to tail-risk evaluation.
item.dc:creator: Weijia Han, Zhi Huang, Lisha Qu, Yuanyuan Tan, Jiayue Meng

item.title: Vehicle clustering and resource scheduling scheme based on collaborative perception of wireless resources
item.description: arXiv:2610.41423v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cellular Vehicle-to-Everything(C-V2X) sidelink communication allows autonomous resource selection via distributed scheduling without base station coverage. However, the limited perception of wireless resources may lead to resource allocation conflicts, especially when wireless resources are relatively scarce. In this paper, we propose a distributed clustering and resource scheduling scheme based on collaborative perception of wireless resources. The scheme innovatively integrates wireless resource sensing states into the clustering process. Based on the constructed vehicle clustering structure, the cluster heads fuse the distributed perception data of wireless resources from cluster members to generate more accurate collaborative perception results of the environment where the clusters are located, so as to support more reliable resource scheduling and reduce resource allocation conflicts. Simulation results show that the proposed scheme achieves higher topological stability than conventional clustering schemes based solely on mobility, and superior communication performance compared to the autonomous resource allocation mechanism of C-V2X.
item.dc:creator: Jingbin Lu, Zhonghui Pei, Long Xie, Zhengxiong Hu, Run Wang, Yuntao Wu

item.title: Physically Constrained Kinematic Calibration for High-Precision Robotic Needle Guidance
item.description: arXiv:2610.41429v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Percutaneous needle insertion is a common practice in minimally invasive procedures whose clinical success depends on accurate needle placement. However, achieving the necessary precision is a challenge for manual operators. Robotic assistance can improve targeting accuracy and reduce operator dependence, but residual millimeter-scale errors persist because nominal kinematic models do not fully represent the physical manipulator. This paper presents a robust bound-constrained kinematic calibration method designed to improve positional accuracy for a 6-Degree-of-Freedom (6-DoF) robotic needle-guidance manipulator. The approach uses physically plausible parameter ranges to regularize a compact 19-parameter geometric identification model. By treating these bounds as active optimization constraints rather than mere numerical safeguards, the framework effectively mitigates parameter coupling and overfitting, ensuring highly stable parameter identification. In simulation, the proposed method reduced end-effector Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) from 3.422 mm to 0.690 mm (a 79.8% improvement). In benchtop hardware experiments, the calibrated model achieved sub-millimeter validation accuracy, including 0.865 mm RMSE in experimental trajectory validation and 0.610 mm RMSE in a coordinate-lattice verification task. These results demonstrate that physically constrained kinematic calibration can enhance robotic needle-targeting accuracy, establishing a high-precision foundation for future clinical applications.
item.dc:creator: Prabhu Nithin Gollapudi, Andreas Maier, Franziska Mathis-Ullrich, Water Zhao, Jia Wang, Siming Bayer

item.title: GNSS Receiver Operating Point Comparison Between Vector and Scalar Tracking Under High-Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.41498v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper presents a measurement noise adaptation mechanism for Kalman filter-based carrier tracking in a navigation-aided GNSS receiver designed for launch-vehicle applications. The tracking loop is tuned for 20\,g acceleration steps, which requires a wide bandwidth that makes the loop vulnerable to noise-driven pull-out at low carrier-to-noise density ratios. To resolve this tradeoff, the measurement noise covariance, $R$, is inflated via a two-layer gate: a sigmoid envelope keyed to the signal $C/N_0$, modulated by a dynamics indicator derived from the discriminator output statistics of the Loop Bandwidth Control Algorithm. During noise-dominated periods the gate inflates~$R$, reducing the Kalman gain so the filter coasts on the navigation-aided prediction; when dynamics are detected the gate opens within one epoch, restoring the high-bandwidth tuning. The navigation aiding is formulated as a stochastic control input whose uncertainty is propagated from the navigation EKF covariance. Simulation results on a 20\,g acceleration step scenario show that the adapted vector architecture doubles the lock-retention rate relative to the standalone scalar filter at $C/N_0 = 31$\,dB-Hz. The receiver is implemented in MSGR, an open-source MATLAB GNSS software-defined receiver.
item.dc:creator: J. Ferm\'in Llorente, Ernesto M. L\'opez, Javier A. Smidt, Pedro A. Roncagliolo

item.title: Contact-based optimization for collision-free motion planning for a million robots
item.description: arXiv:2610.41548v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-agent robotic systems have attracted growing interest in recent years, with applications ranging from coordinated drone shows to autonomous operations on land, in the air, and on water. At the planning level, robot motion is often modeled using double-integrator dynamics (with low-level controllers handling the physical dynamics during execution) with a minimum-energy objective subject to collision-avoidance constraints and limits on position, velocity, and acceleration. The complexity of the problem resides in the constraints, which couple the trajectories and make the optimization problem nonconvex. Existing numerical approaches typically discretize and optimize entire trajectories, which becomes expensive for large fleets. We exploit the structure of optimal trajectories by organizing optimization around contacts, at which robots reach the minimum allowed separation. We formulate a coupled algebraic system in contact variables and reconstruct trajectories analytically between contacts. Our algorithm, sequential contact insertion (SCI), starts from unconstrained trajectories, inserts contacts at separation violations, and jointly adjusts their times and states. Numerical experiments demonstrate planning for one million robots in minutes and thousands of robots in fractions of a second. On problems feasible for a fixed-grid sequential convex programming baseline, SCI achieves median speedups of several orders of magnitude at matching solution accuracy.
item.dc:creator: Jan Kamm, Antonio Terpin, Raffaello D'Andrea

item.title: A complete analytical characterization of optimal collision-free motion for two robots
item.description: arXiv:2610.41558v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Collision-free motion planning for multi-agent robotic systems remains an active research area because of the complexity of coordinating robot trajectories, with applications ranging from coordinated drone shows to autonomous operations on land, in the air, and on water. Importantly, the analytical difficulty of nonconvex collision-avoidance constraints has so far driven the development of exclusively numerical methods. We derive a complete analytical characterization of the optimal trajectories for two robots that start and end at rest, under double-integrator dynamics and a squared-acceleration objective. We prove that these trajectories belong to eight distinct contact families and determine which family applies for each configuration of initial and final positions. We analyze the geometrical properties of the optimal trajectories, provide a numerical algorithm for computing them, and discuss how these insights may improve the performance of existing numerical trajectory optimizers.
item.dc:creator: Jan Kamm, Antonio Terpin, Raffaello D'Andrea

item.title: Distributed Zeroth-Order Composite Finite-Sum Optimization via Incremental Variance Reduction
item.description: arXiv:2610.41615v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study decentralized composite finite-sum optimization over a fixed connected undirected network, where agents access local component functions through function evaluations and share a possibly nonsmooth convex regularizer. In this setting, standard two-point gradient estimators can retain nonvanishing variance at a solution, complicating their integration with gradient tracking. We propose Distributed Zeroth-Order Incremental Variance Reduction (Distributed ZIVR), which combines incrementally updated component-gradient estimates with a proximal gradient-tracking scheme. The method admits an implementation using a constant number of function evaluations per agent at every iteration, without intermittent full-component or full-coordinate refreshes. For convex smooth component functions and strongly convex local averages, we establish linear convergence up to a controllable finite-difference error. With the finite-difference radius chosen for the target accuracy, Chebyshev-accelerated mixing yields a per-agent oracle complexity of $\widetilde{O}(d(m+\kappa)\log(1/\epsilon))$ for expected squared solution error $\epsilon$, where $d$ is the dimension, $m$ is the number of components per agent, and $\kappa$ is the condition number. This matches the centralized ZIVR oracle bound, while the communication bound has only an inverse square-root dependence on the network spectral gap. Experiments on logistic and robust regression demonstrate rapid reduction of solution and consensus errors.
item.dc:creator: Silan Zhang, Yujie Tang

item.title: Clinical-Protocol-Aware Cyber Resilience for Connected Clinical Technologies Under AI-Enabled Adversarial Conditions
item.description: arXiv:2610.41784v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Healthcare increasingly relies on connected medical devices, clinical information systems, cloud services, and distributed-care technologies, creating cybersecurity risks across clinical workflows. AI-enabled capabilities can accelerate vulnerability discovery and attack-path analysis, increasing the need to limit compromise propagation. This paper proposes a clinical-protocol-aware cyber-resilience framework based on bounded clinical micro-networks and controlled interconnections. The framework integrates clinical factors into cybersecurity design, management, and evaluation, covering prevention, containment, and incident response. A parameterized Monte Carlo simulation distinguishes technical cyber exposure from modeled clinical consequence. Experiments investigate architectural connectivity, adversarial capability, security controls, protocol dependency, risk alignment, communication directionality, lifecycle integration, and response timing. Under the simulation assumptions, connected architecture increases mean cyber exposure by 56.3% relative to segmented architecture, while combined prevention and containment reduce exposure by 60.1% relative to no controls. Increasing protocol dependency raises the modeled clinical-impact index from 1.021 to 7.567 without changing mean cyber exposure, demonstrating that technical exposure and clinical consequence can diverge. Risk-alignment experiments further indicate higher modeled clinical impact when greater technical risk corresponds to greater clinical significance. The findings support comparative architectural analysis, not calibrated estimates of real-world cyber risk, control effectiveness, or patient harm. The framework provides a clinical-context-aware approach to security-boundary design, control prioritization, and coordinated containment in connected healthcare environments.

item.title: Proof-Carrying Evolution: Black-Box Search, White-Box Flight
item.description: arXiv:2610.42043v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study whether a language model can help design controllers whose behavior can be formally checked. In proof-carrying evolution (PCE), a search proposes controllers together with their certificates. Their mathematical forms are fixed; a proposer chooses their numerical parameters together. Certificate checks guide selection, and only a certified candidate can be returned. The deployed artifact is a control law and its certificate; the language model is used only during design. We compare four language models with classical search and synthesis on docking under a speed limit, pursuit of a maneuvering target, and attitude control on SO(3), using paired runs and shared proposal allowances. Certificates are checked in exact rational arithmetic during search on the linear problems. On SO(3), the search uses floating-point checks, followed by exact re-verification of every reported champion. The best run of each method also receives Lean 4 proofs of its stated control properties. On the linear problems, the strongest models beat the standard classical baselines on every run, but a classical optimizer that chooses certificates for the same objective closes most of that lead. Among the cited pursuit champions, the ranking does not survive a change from Euler to zero-order-hold dynamics. On SO(3), no model detectably outperforms CMA-ES when mixed with classical mutation. When models write every proposal, one tested model improves on CMA-ES and the other performs worse than its mixed variant. All search medians remain below the hand-tuned law. In a docking control with the objective and mutation operator held fixed, retaining certified candidates yields new certified designs in every run; removing this rule yields none.
